function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run recipe** that you can paste into a terminal (or copy into a script) to finish the whole workflow you described.  
It assumes you already have SSH access to the repo (`git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`) and that you have the required secrets (`DOCKER_USERNAME`, `DOCKER_PASSWORD`, `KUBECONFIG`) added to the repository’s *Settings → Secrets* page.

> **NOTE** – The helper function `create_a_docker_file` is designed for Python projects, so we’ll hand‑craft the Dockerfile instead.  
> The helper `create_kubernetes_yaml_file` could be used, but the content below is written out explicitly so you can see exactly what gets committed.

---

## 1️⃣  Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣  Analyse the repo & create the artefacts

### 2.1  Dockerfile

Create a `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo:

```bash
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
# Use official Node.js LTS image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
EOF
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small, secure, and contains the latest LTS of Node.js.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a reproducible install from `package-lock.json`.  
> * The app is expected to listen on port **3000** (the common default for Express/Node apps). Adjust if your app uses a different port.

### 2.2  Kubernetes YAML

Create a `k8s/k8s.yaml` file that contains both the Deployment and Service:

```bash
mkdir -p k8s
cat > k8s/k8s.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
EOF
```

> **Explanation**  
> * **Deployment** – 2 replicas, exposing container port 3000.  
> * **Service** – ClusterIP (internal only), mapping external port 80 to target port 3000.  
> * Image tag is `latest`; you’ll override this in the CI workflow with the commit SHA.

### 2.3  GitHub Actions workflow

Create a workflow that builds the Docker image, pushes it to Docker Hub, and deploys to Kubernetes:

```bash
mkdir -p .github/workflows
cat > .github/workflows/ci.yml <<'EOF'
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v3
      with:
        node-version: '18'

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
        echo "${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}" | docker login -u "${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}" --password-stdin
        docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v1
      with:
        manifests: |
          ./k8s/k8s.yaml
        images: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
        kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
EOF
```

> **What this workflow does**  
> 1. Checks out the repo.  
> 2. Sets up Node.js 18.  
> 3. Installs deps and runs tests (`npm test`).  
> 4. Builds a Docker image tagged with the commit SHA, logs in to Docker Hub using secrets, and pushes it.  
> 5. Uses the Azure/K8s‑deploy action to apply the `k8s/k8s.yaml` manifest, automatically replacing the image tag with the new SHA.  

> **Prerequisites**  
> * Add `DOCKER_USERNAME` and `DOCKER_PASSWORD` as *Repository secrets*.  
> * Add `KUBECONFIG` (base64‑encoded kubeconfig) as a *Repository secret*.

---

## 3️⃣  Commit & push the changes

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, and GitHub Actions workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically, building the image, pushing it to Docker Hub, and deploying the updated image to your Kubernetes cluster.

---

### Quick sanity check

After the workflow completes, you can verify:

```bash
# List images in Docker Hub (replace <username> with your Docker Hub username)
docker pull zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:<sha>
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:<sha>

# Verify Kubernetes rollout
kubectl get deployments
kubectl get services
```

That’s it! You now have a fully automated CI/CD pipeline for the `nodejs-welcome` repo. Happy coding!
